map.An Axiom City episode — Lessons 3-1 & 3-: An Axiom City episode — Lessons 3-1 & 3-2 in one sitting, with three gates. Solve the math to move the story.
map.Race season status: ON. Training camp st: Race season: ON. Training camp: 06:00. Crew: mostly awake.
map.Previously: on a rained-out field day, f: Last time: on a rainy field day, four sixth graders woke VEX in the old observatory. VEX is a piece of Ada Vex's Pattern Engine. Now race season starts. The Courier Cup, the bike relay that pays for the library, is one week away. Training camp opens at dawn.
map.The old depot lot, dawn. Bikes on the ra: The old depot lot, at dawn. Bikes on the rack. Paint on the table. Team Torque is already watching.
map.It's not cute, Bram, it's a recipe: two: It is not cute, Bram. It is a recipe: two parts sky-blue to five parts white. Courier blue. I love this color.
Distortion forecast for race day: high. Today's forecast: paint, pedals, and proportions. Mixing is math, crew. Get it wrong and the flag looks like chalk.
map.The paint table. One recipe card, many c: The paint table. One recipe card, many cans, no room for mistakes.
map.A ratio, not a riddle: 2 cans of blue fo: A ratio, not a riddle: 2 cans of blue for every 5 of white. Say it like a heartbeat: two FOR five.
map.The trim taught me the rule. Gray to amb: The trim taught me the rule. Gray to amber is 1 to 3. I doubled it once, 2 and 6, and the shade did not change. Multiply BOTH numbers or repaint everything.
map.Definition loaded: a ratio compares amou: Definition: a ratio compares amounts. 1:3 is part-to-PART: gray against amber. The whole trim batch is 1 + 3 = 4 parts, so gray-to-WHOLE is 1:4. Same paint, two comparisons.
map.A ratio compares part to part (gray:ambe: A ratio compares part to part (gray:amber, 1:3) or part to whole (gray:all the trim paint, 1:4). To scale a batch, multiply every part by the same number.
map.Reader — you're our fifth crew member. T: Reader, you are our fifth crew member. The flag needs a TRIPLE batch of Courier blue. Pour it right.
map.Courier blue is mixed 2 parts blue : 5 p: Courier blue is 2 parts blue : 5 parts white. Chloe needs a TRIPLE batch for the flag. Fill the cans. Then answer the inspector's next question.
map.Conceptual: a ratio keeps its color only: Conceptual: a ratio keeps its color only when BOTH parts scale together. A triple batch repeats the WHOLE recipe three times. A part-to-whole ratio compares one color to everything in the bucket, not to the other color.
map.Procedural: multiply each part of 2:5 by: Procedural: multiply each part of 2:5 by 3. Do blue first, then white. For the next question, add the recipe's parts (blue + white) to get the whole batch. Then write blue : whole.
map.The depot loop. Rohan has a stopwatch an: The depot loop. Rohan has a stopwatch and a clipboard. Juno, the new courier from Harbor Row, wants the best tryout of her life.
map.Tryout logged! Chloe: 5.4 km in 18 minut: Tryout logged! Chloe: 5.4 km in 18 minutes. Juno: 4.4 km in 11. Two riders, two very different rides.
map.Shorter ride, I know. Don't read the odo: I know, my ride was shorter. Do not read the odometer. Ask the stopwatch.
map.Definition loaded: a rate compares two d: Definition: a rate compares two different units, kilometers AND minutes. Divide distance by time. That is the unit rate, km per ONE minute. One number per rider.
map.Like my warm-up: 2 km in 8 minutes. 2 ÷: Like my warm-up: 2 km in 8 minutes. 2 ÷ 8 = 0.25 km a minute. The decimal does not care how long you rode.
map.A rate compares different units; a unit: A rate compares different units. A unit rate changes it to "per one," like km per 1 minute. Then any two riders can be compared fairly.
map.Reader — run the division. Two unit rate: Reader, do the division. Two unit rates, one anchor leg. Who takes it?
map.Time-trial log: Chloe — 5.4 km in 18 min: Time-trial log: Chloe — 5.4 km in 18 min. Juno — 4.4 km in 11 min. Find each unit rate in km per minute. Then pick the anchor.
map.Conceptual: raw distance can't crown a r: Conceptual: distance alone cannot pick a winner, because the rides took different times. A unit rate says how far ONE minute takes each rider, so rides compare fairly.
map.Procedural: divide distance by time — Ch: Procedural: divide distance by time. Chloe: 5.4 ÷ 18. Juno: 4.4 ÷ 11. Write each as a decimal of kilometers per minute. The bigger decimal covers more road every minute.
map.Farther in MORE minutes, Bram. Speed is: Farther in MORE minutes, Bram. Speed is distance PER minute. The stopwatch wins every time.
map.Welcome to the crew, Juno. You bring the: Welcome to the crew, Juno. You bring the legs. The math brought the proof.
map.The supply shed, late afternoon. Race ru: The supply shed, late afternoon. Race rule #12: every water station has 3 bottles for every 2 riders.
map.Three bottles per TWO riders — so the or: Three bottles per TWO riders, so the order grows by rider-pairs. Count the pairs. Then give each pair its three bottles.
map.And pack prices are decoys. Boss math is: Pack prices fool you. The real math is the price of ONE bottle. Divide the tag price by the pack.
map.Demo from Kofi's juice run: a 6-pack for: Example from Kofi's juice run: a 6-pack for $7.20 → 7.20 ÷ 6 = $1.20 per bottle. The shelf tag is loud. The unit price tells the truth.
map.A unit price is a unit rate in dollars:: A unit price is a unit rate in dollars: cost ÷ count = price of ONE. Compare prices per one, not pack tags.
map.Sundown. The order form is due at the ra: Sundown. The order form is due at the race office tonight. Bram leans on the doorframe and smirks.
map.Torque's order took five minutes. Bet yo: Torque's order took five minutes. I bet your crew spends the library's money by breakfast. I triple bet you cannot show the work.
map.Reader — three locks. Fill the form. Mak: Reader, three locks. Fill the form. Make every coin count.
map.Boss Gate: scale the 3:2 bottle ratio to: Boss Gate: scale the 3:2 bottle ratio to all the riders. Price ONE bottle. Then pick the pack that saves the library's money.
map.The race office form. 24 riders register: The race office form. 24 riders signed up. Each water station has 3 bottles for every 2 riders. The shop sells bottles 5 for $7.50 or 4 for $6.40. Three locks:
map.Conceptual: Lock 1 scales a ratio — 3:2: Conceptual: Lock 1 scales a ratio. 3:2 stays 3:2 however many riders sign up, so think in groups of two riders. Locks 2 and 3 are unit prices. A pack tag means little until you know the cost of ONE bottle.
map.Procedural: Lock 1 — 24 riders ÷ 2 rider: Procedural: Lock 1: 24 riders ÷ 2 riders per group, then 3 bottles for every group. Lock 2: divide $7.50 by 5. Lock 3: the 4-pack already shows its price per bottle. Compare it with Lock 2. Pick the cheaper bottle.
map.Camp's done. But race day feeds SIXTY vo: Camp is done. But race day feeds SIXTY volunteers. Someone must scale Ms. Ortiz's whole recipe table.
map.New distortion humming at the main stage: A new distortion hums at the main stage. It grows in rows and columns. To be continued…
map.Ratio.2:5 means 2 of this for every 5 of: Ratio.2:5 means 2 of this for every 5 of that. Scale a batch by MULTIPLYING both parts by the same number. Part-to-whole compares one part to all the parts together.
map.Rate & unit rate.A rate pairs two differ: Rate & unit rate.A rate pairs two different units (km and minutes). Divide to get the per-ONE number, km per minute. Then riders of any distance compare fairly.
Unit price.Cost ÷ count = price of one. The smaller price per one is the better deal, whatever the pack tag says.
map.completed Unit 3 · Episode 1: Mix & Meas: finished Unit 3 · Episode 1: Mix & Measure and showed they know ratios, rates and unit rates.
map.Thank you for riding with the crew. Epis: Thank you for riding with the crew. Episode 2 is already being built, in rows and columns.
map.Different bucket — banner paint, green:g: New bucket: banner paint, green:gold = 3:5. A DOUBLE batch multiplies both parts by 2 → 6 green, 10 gold. Same color, bigger bucket.
map.Part-to-whole for that recipe: the bucke: Part-to-whole for that recipe: the bucket has 3 + 5 = 8 parts, so green-to-whole is 3:8. Green against ALL the paint.
map.Your turn — same idea, different numbers: Your turn. Same idea, new numbers:
map.Different tryout — scooters. Scooter A c: New tryout: scooters. Scooter A goes 4.5 km in 9 minutes: 4.5 ÷ 9 = 0.5 km per minute.
map.Scooter B covers 5 km in 25 minutes: 5 ÷: Scooter B goes 5 km in 25 minutes: 5 ÷ 25 = 0.2 km per minute. B went farther, but slower per minute.
map.Compare the per-minute decimals, not the: Compare the per-minute decimals, not the trip lengths. 0.5 is more than 0.2, so A is quicker even though its ride was shorter.
map.Scooter C covers 3 km in 6 minutes — wha: Scooter C goes 3 km in 6 minutes. What is its unit rate in km per minute?
map.Different shed — snack bars at 5 bars fo: New shed: snack bars, 5 bars for every 2 riders. For 8 riders: 8 ÷ 2 = 4 groups, then 4 × 5 = 20 bars. Scale the ratio by groups.
map.Better deal: a 3-pack at $4.20 runs 4.20: Better deal? A 3-pack at $4.20 is 4.20 ÷ 3 = $1.40 per bar, so the 4-pack wins. It is cheaper PER BAR, whatever the pack size.
map.Pour something first — both cans need a: Pour something first. Both cans need a number.
map.Those cans went in by ADDING — the same: Those cans were made by ADDING. Adding the same amount to each color keeps the DIFFERENCE, not the ratio. A triple batch multiplies BOTH parts of 2:5 by the same number.
map.Not Courier blue yet. A triple batch mea: Not Courier blue yet. A triple batch means the whole 2:5 recipe is made three times. Scale each part again.
map.Cans are perfect! Now tag the follow-up: Cans are perfect! Now the next one: blue compared to the TOTAL paint.
map.2:5 compares blue to WHITE — part to par: 2:5 compares blue to WHITE, part to part. The next question asks for blue against ALL the paint in the bucket.
map.That's the WHITE share of the bucket. Th: That is the WHITE share. The next question asks about blue.
map.Order matters: that ratio reads total-to: Order matters: that ratio is total-to-blue. Flip it.
map.Triple-true! 6 blue and 15 white still s: Triple-true! 6 blue and 15 white are still 2:5. A bucket holds 2 + 5 = 7 parts, so blue-to-total is 2:7. The flag dries a bright Courier blue.
map.Divide first — each rider needs a km-per: Divide first. Each rider needs a km-per-minute number.
map.Re-run the division: kilometers ÷ minute: Do the division again: kilometers ÷ minutes, one rider at a time. Keep it as a decimal.
Rates are done. Now pick the anchor.
map.Look again — 5.4 km is the longer RIDE,: Look again. 5.4 km is the longer RIDE, not the faster rider. Which decimal gives more road in one minute?
map.0.4 km per minute beats 0.3. Juno takes: 0.4 km per minute is more than 0.3. Juno takes the anchor leg. The stopwatch never brags. It just divides.
map.Lock 1 first — the bottle count drives t: Lock 1 first. The bottle count drives the whole order.
map.Lock 1 holds. Flipped! 3 is the BOTTLE s: Lock 1 is shut. Flipped! 3 is the BOTTLE side of 3:2. Each group is 2 RIDERS. Count rider-pairs first.
map.Lock 1 holds. 12 is the number of rider-: Lock 1 is shut. 12 is the number of rider-PAIRS. Each pair still needs its 3 bottles.
map.Lock 1 holds. That would be 3 bottles pe: Lock 1 is shut. That would be 3 bottles per ONE rider. The ratio says 3 per TWO riders.
map.Lock 1 holds. Split 24 riders into group: Lock 1 is shut. Split 24 riders into groups of 2. Then give each group its 3 bottles.
map.Lock 2 holds. $7.50 split across 5 bottl: Lock 2 is shut. $7.50 split across 5 bottles. Divide, and keep the decimal.
map.Lock 3 holds. $1.60 each is printed righ: Lock 3 is shut. $1.60 each is printed on the 4-pack. Lock 2 just showed you what ONE bottle from the 5-pack costs. The smaller price per bottle wins.
map.ALL LOCKS OPEN. 24 riders → 12 pairs → 3: ALL LOCKS OPEN. 24 riders → 12 pairs → 36 bottles. $7.50 ÷ 5 = $1.50 a bottle, and $1.50 is less than $1.60. The 5-packs save the library's prize money. Order filed. Bram, please hush.
Yes! Now go back and open that gate.
